title: Writing on the Guitar
intro: The guitar suggests songs through its shapes: open chords that ring, riffs under the fingers, and tunings that change everything. This page covers the patterns guitarists write with, and how the instrument's habits shape the music.

blocks.text: Keep the strumming hand moving down and up in steady eighths (or sixteenths) and choose which strokes hit the strings. Common patterns in 4/4 (D = down, U = up, - = miss):

items: D - D U - U D U: the all-purpose pop/folk pattern.
D - D - D U D U: driving, for rock eighths.
D - - U - U D U: syncopated, with the beat-3 push.
Muting the strings on beats 2 and 4 with the strumming hand makes a percussive backbeat (the 'chuck').

widget.title: Strummed C–G–Am–F (D – D U – U D U)

blocks.text: Fingerpicking separates bass and treble: the thumb plays bass notes on strings 6–4, the fingers play the upper strings. Travis picking alternates two bass notes (root and fifth, or root and third) on every beat while the fingers pick between them. Arpeggio patterns (thumb, then i–m–a up the strings) suit slow ballads.

widget.title: Travis picking on C (thumb alternates strings 5 and 4)

blocks.text: A riff is a short repeated figure, usually on the low strings, that carries a song by itself. Riffs come from the minor pentatonic (see Scales on the Guitar (#/arts/guitar/guitar-theory/scales)) and from power chords (see Chord Voicings (#/arts/guitar/guitar-theory/chord-voicings)): two-finger shapes that move easily, so rhythm and placement matter more than harmony. Write a riff by fixing a rhythm first, then choosing notes from the box.

widget.title: A riff in E minor pentatonic

items: Let open strings ring against moving shapes: G (320033) → Cadd9 (x32033) → Dsus4 (xx0233) → Em7 (022033) keeps the top two strings on D and G the whole time; ringing common tones glue the changes together.

A capo changes the key without changing the shapes, so you can write in the guitar's resonant open-chord keys and still fit a singer (see Tuning, Tab and Chord Diagrams (#/arts/guitar/tuning-and-tab)).
Alternate tunings (DADGAD, open G, drop D) put new chords under the same fingers; many writers use them precisely because familiar shapes stop working and new ideas appear.

blocks.text: How the guitar shapes a song

Guitar-written songs lean on the open-chord keys (E, A, D, G, C), on chords with ringing open strings (sus2, add9, sus4), and on progressions that are easy to finger (I–IV–V, I–♭VII–IV). Writing a song away from the guitar, at the piano or by singing, is a good way to escape those habits; bringing it back to the guitar afterwards then becomes an arranging problem (see Piano and Guitar Together (#/arts/songwriting/piano-and-guitar-together)).

blocks.title: Common tones
blocks.text: Which notes stay the same between G (320033) and Cadd9 (x32033)?
solution: G (320033): G B D G D G. Cadd9 (x32033): C E G D G. Strings 1 and 2 are fretted at 3 in both (G and D) and the open G string is shared, so G, D and G ring through the change while only the bass strings move (G–B–D to x–C–E).
blocks.answer: The open G string and the top two strings (D and G at fret 3)
